Carbon residue collected from the interior of the plasma reformer after high-flow operation. The presence of light, removable carbon deposits confirm methane decomposition according to CH → C + 2H 4 2 while indicating that most solid carbon was carried downstream by gas flow, limiting reactor fouling. A localized thermal anomaly was observed during high-flow testing beyond 250 SLPM. The event involved partial surface melting of a polymeric insulator located at the high-voltage electrode interface, as shown in Figure 15. This degradation was traced to capacitive charge buildup within the insulating assembly surrounding the high-voltage feedthrough. The phenomenon occurred when the multilayer Kapton insulation, originally intended to provide secondary dielectric protection, enabled charge accumulation under high-repetition pulse operation. As the stored charge discharged across a small gas gap, it caused localized heating and minor damage to the insulator surface. To correct this issue, the redundant Kapton layer was removed, and the electrical connector was redesigned to reduce electric-field concentration and eliminate regions prone to charge trapping. Subsequent testing confirmed that the revised design eliminated further dielectric breakdown or thermal damage, allowing stable high-voltage operation. Overall, the high- flow testing campaign successfully verified the operational envelope of the plasma reformer and confirmed that the system maintained plasma stability, minimal fouling, and consistent electrical performance at realistic engine fuel flow conditions. These findings established confidence in the reformer’s readiness for engine integration. The left image shows the burned region on the insulator surrounding the high-voltage electrode, and the right image shows damage to the Kapton insulation at the conductor tip prior to redesign. 3.4 Engine Testing on the AJAX 2802 ULE Engine-scale testing was conducted to evaluate the plasma reformer’s impact on methane slip under realistic combustion conditions. The experiments were performed using a Cooper AJAX 2802 ULE two-cylinder, large-bore natural-gas engine rated at 384 bhp and operating at 440 rpm. This engine type represents a standard configuration widely used for midstream natural-gas compression. The plasma reformer was integrated into the engine’s pre-chamber combustion fuel supply line so that the reformed fuel mixture with hydrogen (H ) and short-chain hydrocarbons 2 (C H ) could participate in pre-chamber combustion.
